entries.summary: Former President Talon was elected Senate president just months after handing power to his protégé, President Wadagni, while Benin and Nigeria continued to deepen security cooperation amid mounting cross-border insecurity.

President Capt. Traoré continued to assert sole authority amid the prolonged disappearance of top officials in military government; JNIM launched further attacks on government forces and rival Islamic State militants.
President Ndayishimiye faced mounting pressure from army commanders to withdraw troops from DR Congo, and the 2027 presidential race began to take shape.

President Biya returned to Cameroon after a record 73-day absence, easing immediate concerns about a potential power vacuum, while armed conflicts continued to exact a heavy toll in the Anglophone regions and the Far North.

The government and UN mission (MINUSCA) advanced plans to transfer some of the mission’s responsibilities to national authorities as part of its gradual drawdown, while insecurity persisted in several regions.

Authorities accused the Sudanese army of launching airstrikes inside Chadian territory as the war in Sudan continued to spill across borders; President Déby pardoned prominent political opponents in a move framed as a gesture toward national reconciliation.
Some opposition parties reshuffled their leadership in a bid to regain political relevance, while a land conflict in the country’s south turned deadly.

Kinshasa and the Rwanda-backed M23 agreed on a roadmap for further negotiations and implementation of commitments under the Doha process; the main opposition coalition rejected President Tshisekedi’s national dialogue process.
Asmara put its forces on high alert following clashes in Ethiopia’s Tigray region and reiterated that Red Sea security should primarily be the responsibility of littoral states.

Heavy clashes erupted in Tigray between the military and forces aligned with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), while federal drone strikes hit sites across the region, including Mekelle, in the first such attack on the regional capital since the 2022 peace deal.
President Doumbouya travelled abroad, fuelling speculation about his health and actual grip on power, and later dismissed scores of soldiers amid reports of tensions within the military.
The country held a referendum on a proposed constitution that would replace the semi-presidential system with a presidential one.
Political violence continued to intensify ahead of the 2027 presidential election as suspected goons brutally disrupted opposition meetings, leaving several dead.

Al-Qaeda militants retained the capacity to strike strategic military positions despite a government counteroffensive; meanwhile, Azawad rebels released captured soldiers and transitional President Gen. Goïta pardoned a French intelligence officer.

Islamic State militants abducted dozens of civilians and remained active across large swathes of northern Cabo Delgado province, while the Supreme Court summoned opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane to stand trial.
Gunfire and explosions rocked the capital, Niamey, as a group of soldiers attempted to stage a mutiny, marking the latest challenge to General Abdourahamane Tiani’s rule.
Criminal, jihadist and ethnic armed groups killed and abducted hundreds of people in the North West and North Central zones, while jihadist violence remained at a low ebb in the North East.
Addis Ababa and Cairo sparred over dam projects on the Blue Nile.

Kigali and Kinshasa remained at odds over the disarmament of the FDLR rebel group, hindering implementation of the U.S.-brokered peace agreement.

Mogadishu’s state and local election rollout suffered a setback after the Supreme Court annulled the Galmudug results, while political figures aligned with Mogadishu in Puntland and Jubaland switched sides; Al-Shabaab made its first territorial gain of the year.

Senior political and military figures continued to defect between Somaliland and Somalia’s North Eastern state, while Hargeisa stepped up efforts to end a deadly inter-clan conflict in the Awdal region.
Anti-migrant demonstrations reduced in intensity, while criminal violence remained high.

Heavy fighting between government and opposition forces persisted in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, intercommunal attacks left scores dead and hundreds of cattle looted, and the ruling party remained intent on holding elections in December.

The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) made significant gains in Blue Nile state amid reports of growing Ethiopian involvement and counterattacked in North Kordofan following the army’s July advances, as both sides expanded their drone war; peace efforts remained stalled.
The government announced a commission investigating responsibility for the post-October 2025 violence, while Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi resigned amid a growing rift with President Suluhu Hassan.
President Gnassingbé conducted a military reshuffle, while authorities detained French journalists.

President Museveni’s succession continued to fuel tensions as his son, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, announced his intention to run for president in 2031; opposition leader Kizza Besigye’s party launched a campaign to protest his treason trial and continued detention.

Following the 13 August general elections, the political climate deteriorated sharply as security forces carried out a deadly raid on the main opposition candidate’s home before detaining him on treason charges.

President Mnangagwa solidified his grip on power after the July passing of controversial constitutional amendments that extended his term until 2030; succession jockeying continued within the ruling party.

Armed opposition groups intensified attacks against the Taliban, potentially marking the start of a sustained challenge to the de facto rulers; internal Taliban tensions erupted into deadly clashes in the north-eastern Badakhshan province.

Parliament elected the ruling Bangladesh National Party’s (BNP) candidate in the first contested presidential vote in decades, while the government adopted several accountability reforms and navigated tensions with India.
Trade tensions and Washington’s economic warfare against Iran appeared to strain U.S.-China ties ahead of Chinese President Xi’s visit to the U.S. in September.
China continued maritime activity in the disputed East China Sea, while a diplomatic thaw in bilateral ties appeared to be a long way off.
Tit-for-tat attacks between the Naga and Kuki ethnic communities continued in Manipur state, while New Delhi and China made progress in dialogue on the disputed border.

Chief Minister Omar Abdullah continued calls to restore Jammu & Kashmir’s (J&K) statehood on the seventh anniversary of its revocation, while remarks by the U.S. ambassador to India during a visit to J&K sparked Pakistani objections.
Alleged military abuses in Papua sparked local protests demanding accountability, while Jakarta expanded defence ties with Thailand and balanced relations between China and the U.S.
U.S. President Trump abruptly shortened annual military drills with South Korea in an apparent bid to entice North Korea into dialogue, which Pyongyang rejected.

The military attempted to advance in the north and south east, while intensifying airstrikes on opposition-held areas that killed dozens of civilians; the regime courted international support.

Tensions with Kabul remained high amid unabated insurgent violence in the borderlands, while supporters of imprisoned opposition leader Imran Khan staged protests and threatened a march on the capital.
Insecurity persisted in the Bangsamoro region ahead of inaugural elections set for 14 September, while communist rebels faced continued pressure by government forces.
Tensions persisted between Manila and Beijing in South China Sea (SCS), even as Manila signalled openness for potential energy exploration with Beijing.
The government’s judicial reforms triggered domestic and international criticism, as the cabinet approved a long-promised counter-terrorism law.
China maintained its maritime and aerial presence around Taiwan, which held annual military drills and proposed record defence spending in a new budget.
Border tensions with Cambodia remained elevated, as Bangkok took issue with a UN report on human rights in Cambodia; insurgents staged coordinated attacks across the deep south.

Armenia and Azerbaijan, alongside the U.S., issued a joint statement marking one year since the two countries initialled a peace treaty in Washington; meanwhile, the government maintained pressure on opposition figures and announced it would apply for EU membership.

Azerbaijan and Armenia, alongside the U.S., issued a joint statement marking one year since the two countries initialled a peace treaty in Washington, while Baku navigated a turbulent relationship with Moscow.
Tensions with Latvia rose over illegal migration, while Washington said it expected more prisoner releases in the near future.

A series of Facebook posts by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili exposed tensions within the ruling Georgian Dream party, while the government sent fuel shipments to the breakaway region of Abkhazia.
The newly created ruling party, Adilet, secured a widely expected victory in parliamentary elections.

Acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti and opposition leader Lumir Abdixhiku reached agreement on a presidential candidate, while NATO’s decision to reduce its peacekeeping presence in North Mitrovica sparked fresh concern among Kosovo Serbs.

Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan began implementing a land swap as part of the demarcation of their shared border, Bishkek sought to reduce its reliance on Russian fuel exports, and countries in the South Caucasus showed growing interest in Central Asia.

Ukraine’s air war expanded, causing a growing number of civilian casualties and economic disruption, the U.S. intelligence chief travelled to Russia and tensions with Europe ran high; meanwhile, Moscow cracked down on the last remnants of the anti-war opposition.
Insecurity in the Tajik-Afghan borderlands persisted, while Dushanbe sought to reduce its reliance on Russian fuel exports.

The government laid the legal groundwork for the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), marking a significant step forward; Ankara signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, while tensions soared with Israel.

Kyiv and Moscow traded more aerial attacks, killing scores of civilians as Ukraine ran out of air defence missiles and raising concern over global food supplies amid strikes in the Black Sea; meanwhile, front-line fighting remained fierce and President Zelenskyy faced more political challenges at home.

Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan began implementing a land swap as part of the demarcation of their shared border, regional officials sought to deepen cooperation over water resources, and Tashkent bolstered relations with Baku.

President de la Espriella took office promising a tougher stance on security and subsequently launched strikes against armed and criminal groups while reinforcing ties with the U.S., Ecuador and Israel; meanwhile, the country was struck by a 7.4-magnitude earthquake.

The U.S. continued to ramp up pressure on Cuba through its oil blockade, sanctions and increasingly confrontational military rhetoric, fuelling the energy crisis while narrowing the space for diplomacy; Havana defended its planned economic reforms.

The government introduced new security measures amid persistent criminal violence, deploying additional personnel in the capital Quito and assuming control of the city’s surveillance systems; authorities also deepened ties with Argentina and Colombia.
Concerns about the government’s draconian anti-gang measures continued, including over judicial processes and prison conditions, while San Salvador’s relations with Bogotá improved.

Gangs killed dozens of people in a brutal attack on Kenscoff commune, which came as the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) prepared for offensive operations; meanwhile, inter-gang fighting resumed in Port-au-Prince’s Cité Soleil neighbourhood and electoral preparations continued despite slow voter registration.

Violence persisted across high-conflict areas, notably in Sinaloa and Michoacán states, while Washington targeted the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and increased pressure on figures in the ruling Morena party.
The regime faced international criticism over its consolidation of authoritarian rule, while opposition groups reportedly coalesced around a transition plan.

The first round of U.S.-sponsored talks between the interim authorities and part of the opposition produced an agreement on judicial reform, while U.S. President Trump announced that Washington had secured an ownership stake in Venezuela’s oil fields.
Algiers continued to mend ties with Sahelian countries as both Mali and Niger’s transitional prime ministers visited Algeria.
The U.S.-Iran war shifted to the economic domain, offering Bahrain a reprieve from Iranian attacks even as a final settlement remained elusive.

The government responded cautiously to drone strikes at Damietta Port and continued to call for de-escalation in the broader Iran conflict; Cairo also pressed for implementation of the Gaza ceasefire.
After June’s Memorandum of Understanding collapsed, Washington shifted focus from military attacks to a campaign of economic isolation, which could provoke Tehran’s military retaliation.
The government continued its effort to rein in Iran-backed militias before its 30 September deadline as concerns mounted it could provoke a dangerous confrontation.

Israel continued expanding settlements in the West Bank and chipped away at the decades-old status quo on Jerusalem’s Holy Esplanade, while Israeli intransigence derailed nascent progress on the Gaza ceasefire.
After a month-long hiatus, Iran launched a missile barrage at American military sites in Jordan in retaliation for a U.S. attack.
The U.S.-Iran war shifted to the economic domain, offering Kuwait a reprieve from Iranian attacks even as a final settlement remained elusive.
The government and Israel continued security talks without tangible progress, while Israel continued attacks in the south and Hizbollah largely refrained from retaliation.

Drone attacks on energy infrastructure in the country’s west and the assassination of the military intelligence chief in the east revived fears of wider instability, while a U.S.-led initiative to unify the country’s divided institutions made no tangible progress.
Muscat continued negotiations with Iran on reopening the Strait of Hormuz amid growing U.S. pressure to align the arrangement with Washington’s demands.
The U.S.-Iran war shifted to the economic domain, offering Qatar a reprieve from Iranian attacks.
The Houthis intensified pressure on the kingdom, raising the prospect of Riyadh being drawn deeper into Yemen’s conflict; Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed a landmark defence pact.
The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) dissolved itself and its administration in the north east, marking a major step toward integrating with the state; tensions soared between Türkiye and Israel.
Anti-government
As the U.S.-Iran war shifted to the economic domain, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) halted all economic dealings with Tehran.

Ahead of the UN Security Council’s October review of the UN Mission in Western Sahara (MINURSO), Morocco secured a new diplomatic gain as Colombia recognised its sovereignty over the disputed territory.

The Houthis intensified pressure on Saudi Arabia through maritime and cross-border attacks, which could draw Riyadh deeper into the conflict, while escalating hostilities on multiple front lines between Houthi and government forces threaten to reignite all-out civil war.
